h: A ship with a Belfast story
p: HMS Caroline was launched in 1914 at Cammell Laird in Birkenhead, and after her wartime service she found a new role in Belfast, where she spent many decades as a training ship for naval reservists. That long link with the city is part of why she's such a treasured piece of local history today.

How long should you allow? A visit usually takes a couple of hours, depending on how much time you spend reading the displays and chatting with guides. Older children who enjoy exploring tend to love the narrow passages and ladders, while younger ones may need a bit more help on the steep steps.
Wear comfortable shoes with good grip, and bring a warm layer for the open decks and the dockside. If you have mobility concerns, check the access information in advance so you know what to expect.

Right beside the ship is the Thompson Dock and Pump House, the dry dock where Titanic was fitted out before her maiden voyage. Standing in that enormous dock really brings home the scale of the ships built here.

From there, it's an easy walk along the Maritime Mile to Titanic Belfast, the striking museum that tells the story of the famous liner and the city that built her. Nearby, SS Nomadic, Titanic's tender ship, has been restored and is open to visitors. Keep an eye out for Samson and Goliath, the two giant yellow cranes of Harland & Wolff that dominate the skyline and have become symbols of the city's shipbuilding heritage.
